works.title: Tokopedia's Product Launching Platform
works.description: Built a cross-platform design system used across Shopee, Garena, and SeaMoney.

columns.html: Overview
A Project to create a self-serve product launching platform that helps sellers/brand to create their own campaign on their shop.
Objective
The main objective is how to create a seamless platform that sellers can use to make their process of product launching campaign simpler and easier.
🎉 Outcome
An end to end self serve product launching platform is now available to the selected seller in Tokopedia
Bring x times (confidential) higher traffic to brands & Tokopedia as a platform compared to the usual Flash Sale campaign
Total of thousands of products sold out in an (x mins - confidential) in a single campaign
👩‍💻 My Role
Main User Experience Designer for this project
Co-assist a co-design session which involved ~20 people from different function (Business, Product, Engineer, Data Analyst) to help align our vision for the product.
Collaborate and worked together with PMs, Engineer, UI Designer to help bring the design to life
Designed the end to end journey and user flow on the seller's end
Conducted user testing & user in-depth interview on end to end journey.
⚡️ Behind The Product
Project Background
In the first quarter of 2020, Tokopedia has been given the opportunity to work together with some of the most highly requested official brands.

The collaboration was formed to provide these brands with a reliable online platform to launch their products. Considering that the products that they launch have always been a huge hit among collectors and fans of the brand & public, where they usually only lasted 10 - 30 mins before all the products sold out. This collaboration has successfully increased traffic and conversion for both parties.
After the big success of launching and partnering with these brands, we receive a surge in interest from other brands to also have a product launch on our platform.
Key Problem
The sudden surge of interest from brands also comes with some challenges that we need to solve. Since the first iteration of Tokopedia's product launching has to be done manually:

Long time to process and a campaign request from brands A brand needs to wait for several days to launch their product due to manual operational effort. This makes the platform isn't scalable for future business opportunities with brands.
Can’t run multiple launching brands at the same time Since it was done manually, the process will take up too many people & effort to run.

There's a special request from brands to have specific terms and condition An example of this use case is many brands needed to limit/give exclusivity for some of their campaigns. With this request, there's an additional couple of hours for the operational team to validate this rule.

There's no specific entry point where sellers can request to create their product launching campaign Currently, sellers would have to manually reach out to our internal team to request this type of campaign.

works.title: It Takes a Village… But What If Yours Is in Another Country?
works.description: Mom-ing abroad without your people is lonely, and nobody really warns you about it. Here's what it actually feels like (sick days included), plus three small things that have made my days lighter.

blocks.html: TL;DR: Mom-ing abroad without your people is lonely, and nobody really warns you about it. Here's what it actually feels like (sick days included), plus three small things that have made my days lighter.
They say it takes a village to raise a child. Well, nobody told me what happens when your village is in a different country.

First off, to give you context: I'm an Indonesian mom raising a toddler here in Singapore, a.k.a. the little red dot 🇸🇬. When I became a mom abroad, I had this very romantic picture in my head — grandparents dropping by, an aunt holding the baby so I could shower, a friend sitting across from me with a cup of tea saying, "Yes, it's hard. You're doing fine."
But boy, was I wrong. In reality, it was me, my husband, and a very small human who needed us every minute of every day.
🫂 The loneliness nobody talks about

Let's be real, being a mom far from home is a very specific kind of lonely. It's not that you're never around people — you're literally surrounded by a tiny human's needs all day long. But there's no one who knows you. No one who remembers you from before, who can look at your face and go, "You haven't slept, have you?"
The hardest moments aren't the dramatic ones. They're small, and they're on repeat:
The 3 p.m. kitchen moment. Toddler on my hip, wishing someone would just walk in and take over for ten minutes. (Ten! That's all I ask.)
The family group chat. Everyone gathered for a celebration back home, and I'm liking the photos from another country.
The cousin guilt. My child is growing up without cousins and grandparents in the room.
The adult-conversation drought. Realising I haven't had a proper chat with another grown-up in days.

And underneath all of that, there's a quiet grief. I miss my mom. I miss being mothered myself. I miss the version of parenting where someone else knows the answers — or at least tells me I'm allowed not to.
🤒 There's no sick leave in motherhood
Nothing shows you how alone you are quite like getting sick.

When you have a village, being unwell means someone shows up. Your mom takes the baby for the afternoon, or your sister drops by with soup and stays for a few hours. You get to lie down and just… be sick.

When you don't? You're running a fever while warming a bottle. You're nauseous (or full-on masuk angin) and still chasing a toddler who has zero idea you feel awful. Your body is begging you to stop, but there's no one to hand the baby to. So you keep going, because breakfast, diaper changes, nap time and bedtime stories don't care whether you slept.
Even when my husband takes over after work, the daytime hours are still mine. No email to my manager, no "I'm out today" message can make this job pause. It simply never clocks out.

Being the UX designer that I am, I can't help but see it as a system with no backup — one person, zero redundancy, and no scheduled downtime. Any product team would flag that as a huge risk. In motherhood, we just call it Tuesday.
😔 And then the guilt kicks in

Then comes the second layer: guilt. We chose this move, this adventure, this life abroad. So who am I to complain, right? A lot of us end up swallowing the exhaustion because saying it out loud feels ungrateful.
But here's what I've come to realise:
Two things can be true at once. You can love your life abroad and find motherhood without a village really, really hard.
Missing your people doesn't mean you made the wrong choice. It just means you're human.
💡 What has helped me (and might help you)

I can't build a village overnight (if only there was a shortcut for that), and neither can you. But I've learned that small, deliberate choices can make the days lighter. Quick disclaimer: I'm not a parenting expert — these are simply the three things that have worked for me so far.
🙋‍♀️ Ask your partner to cover you, a few times a day
This isn't about splitting chores or finally getting the laundry done. It's about giving you time that belongs only to you.
How it works: Ask your husband or partner to take over for a short stretch — even 20 to 30 minutes — a few times a day.

The one rule: This time is not for the house. No errands, no dishes, no meal prep. Sit in silence, drink a coffee while it's actually hot, shower without rushing, or just stare out of a window. (All valid.)
On sick days: This is your version of sick leave. Ask for the cover, and take it without guilt.
And say it out loud, because partners can't read minds. "I need a break, can you take over for a bit?" is a complete and reasonable sentence.
🏋️‍♀️ Move your body: workout, good mood

I used to think exercise was a luxury I'd get back to "once things settle down". (Spoiler: things never really settle down.) Then I realised it's one of the fastest ways to shift my mood on a hard day.

It doesn't have to be a big production. A short home workout, a run, or a walk with the stroller can clear your head and give you a little bit of yourself back. Some days it feels like the last thing I have energy for — and those are usually the days it helps the most.
Workout, good mood. Simple as that.
📱 Video call your people, and do it often

Distance is real, but so is technology. Schedule regular video calls with your mom, your sister, your best friend — anyone who makes you feel like you. Let them see your messy hair and your toddler's chaos. Let them pull funny faces at your little one.
It won't replace a hug, but it does remind you that you're not as alone as it feels. Bonus: your child gets to build a real relationship with faraway family, even if it's through a screen.
💛 My final take: you're doing better than you think

If you're a mom living abroad and reading this in the middle of a long, lonely day — hi, I see you. You're not failing. You're doing an enormous job with fewer hands than most people get, and that's not a small thing.
So be gentle with yourself:
→ Ask for the break. Twenty minutes counts.
→ Move your body. Even a stroller walk.
→ Call the people who love you. Messy hair and all.
→ Find your one fellow mama nearby, if you can. Sometimes a village starts with just one friend.
We may not have the village we grew up in, but we can build a smaller one — one call, one break, and one honest conversation at a time.
Thanks for reading my long story until this point :) If you're mom-ing far from home too, reply below and share what's helped you. Let's help a fellow mama out!

intro: I'm Nadya Arizka a product designer based in Singapore with 9 years of experience in product design.

I have developed a passion for user interface and user experience design. I've always enjoyed engaging with people and discovering the secrets to people's relationships with technology which attracted me to learn more about user experience and fell in love with it more each day.
I received a Bachelor's degree in Information Technology. As an IT graduate, knowing basic knowledge about product development has helped me to understand the feasibility of products that I design.
